name: Machiavelli's separation of means from ends (the 'science of success')
plain_explanation: Machiavelli treats politics scientifically: he studies what actually works to gain and keep power, without moralizing about whether the goals pursued are good or bad. Russell argues this makes his method genuinely value-neutral, so that the same science of political success is equally useful to a 'saint' and a 'sinner,' since both must achieve their purposes to accomplish anything.
precise_definition: Russell's reconstruction: 'His political philosophy is scientific and empirical, based upon his own experience of affairs, concerned to set forth the means to assigned ends, regardless of the question whether the ends are to be considered good or bad'; 'Success' means the achievement of your purpose, whatever it may be... the science, once established, will be just as useful to the saint as to the sinner.'
why_it_mattered: This is, for Russell, Machiavelli's central and most defensible innovation, distinguishing him sharply from moralizing political theorists before and after him.
historical_origin: Developed from Machiavelli's direct experience as a Florentine diplomat and observer of fifteenth-century Italian statecraft.
examples: The detailed analysis of Caesar Borgia's methods of conquest and consolidation of power
objections: The science of success is studied more easily in the successes of the wicked than of the good, since successful sinners are historically more numerous than successful saints
competing_positions: Medieval conceptions of 'legitimate' power derived from the Pope or Emperor, or from biblical grounds (e.g., events in the Garden of Eden), which Machiavelli entirely omits
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates later realist and empirical approaches to political theory, including, Russell suggests, applicability to twentieth-century power politics.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly severs political argument from Christian or biblical grounding.
